haiku-low.q1: Only its SHA-256 hash, stored in token_hash. Plaintext appears only in the create response, browser dialog memory, and server memory during the create request.
haiku-low.q2: It cannot. Closing the dialog discards it, and nobody can show it again. The user must revoke it or leave it, then create a new token.
haiku-low.q3: The create request gets 409 "Limit reached, revoke a token first." Nothing is written.
haiku-low.q4: On the first request after the revoke commits, which gets 401. Requests that passed the lookup just before the revoke may still finish.
haiku-low.q5: The same 401 status and the same generic body for unknown, revoked, and expired tokens. The responses do not differ.
haiku-low.q6: The server hashes the presented token with SHA-256 and looks up token_hash. The row is usable only if revoked_at is NULL and expires_at is later than now().
haiku-low.q7: Any API request using the token, when last_used_at is NULL or over an hour old. A conditional UPDATE's WHERE guard allows one write per hour.
haiku-low.q8: The failure is logged with the token id, and the API request still succeeds.
haiku-low.q9: It sets revoked_at and keeps the row. Lists and counts exclude revoked rows, so the token disappears and its name can be reused.
haiku-low.q10: Both return 404. The owner-scoped UPDATE matches zero rows, the same as for a nonexistent id, so nothing changes.
haiku-low.q11: The token exists as a committed row, but nobody has its plaintext. It shows in the list with last used Never. The user revokes it from the list, then creates a new token.

sonnet.q1: It stores only the SHA-256 hash (token_hash) of the token. Plaintext appears only in the create response (browser dialog memory and server memory during the create request); on later API calls it is in the client's Authorization header and server memory for that request. It is never written to DB, logs, analytics or cache.
sonnet.q2: They cannot. Closing the dialog discards it, nothing can show it again (not even support or engineering). The user must create a new token.
sonnet.q3: The server returns 409 'Limit reached, revoke a token first'. The transaction is rolled back and nothing is written.
sonnet.q4: On the very next request. Every request that starts after the revoke commits gets 401 (no cache; each request reads api_tokens). A request that passed the lookup just before the revoke committed may still finish.
sonnet.q5: All get the same 401 status with the same generic body, so the responses do not differ (this also covers missing or malformed tokens).
sonnet.q6: It checks the header format (pat_ prefix, length 36), computes the SHA-256 of the presented token, and looks up api_tokens by token_hash. The record is usable only if revoked_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now(). The request then runs as the user_id on that row.
sonnet.q7: A successful token lookup where last_used_at is NULL or older than 1 hour triggers UPDATE last_used_at = now(). The guard is in the UPDATE's WHERE clause (last_used_at IS NULL OR last_used_at < now() - 1 hour), so concurrent requests race on it and only one writes; no app-level cache or lock is needed.
sonnet.q8: The API request still succeeds. The failed write is logged with the token id.
sonnet.q9: It sets revoked_at = now() on the row; the row is not deleted (kept for audit, and the name becomes free for reuse). Revoked tokens are no longer active, so they are left out of the list (and of the limit count and name check).
sonnet.q10: Both cases give 0 rows updated and a 404 (identical to a nonexistent id, so other users' ids cannot be probed); the page refreshes the list. Revoke is idempotent.
sonnet.q11: The row is already committed, so an orphan token exists that nobody has the plaintext for. The response cannot be replayed. The UI shows 'Could not confirm. Check the list below before retrying'. The user checks the list (the new name appears with last used Never), revokes the orphan, then creates again. If ignored, the orphan counts toward the limit of 10, blocks the same name, and expires on its own after 90 days.
